title: MotionSites core prompt grammar
text: Most high-performing prompts follow this order: 1) one-sentence build brief with scope, brand, stack, and mood; 2) tech stack and dependency contract; 3) fonts and color system; 4) assets and media URLs with local-vs-remote rules; 5) reusable helper components or animation primitives; 6) exact section-by-section layout with copy, classes, spacing, hierarchy, and states; 7) behavior logic and interactions; 8) responsive breakpoints; 9) acceptance checklist. The stronger prompts are explicit about exact copy, exact URLs, exact classes, and exact animation timing.

title: Output contract that most prompts target
text: The target output is usually a single React page or section in Vite with Tailwind CSS, often TypeScript, with one App.tsx or a named section component. The prompt specifies exact JSX hierarchy, utility classes, motion states, dependencies, and often file-level requirements such as index.html fonts, Tailwind config, CSS variables, and helper components. This means the prompt is not just descriptive; it is a constrained implementation spec.

title: Prompt taxonomy: full site vs page vs section vs component
text: There are four useful buckets for ingestion: full-site or landing-page prompts that define multiple sections and shared systems; page prompts that define a hero or standalone page; section prompts such as FAQ, pricing, about, footer, testimonials, forms; component prompts such as carousels, cards, tabs, loaders. Retrieval should distinguish these because full-site prompts encode shared brand systems while section prompts encode local layout and interaction patterns.

title: Brand system requirements inside prompts
text: Strong prompts always pin down brand voice and art direction early: company name, audience, tone, aesthetic adjectives, key promise, and sometimes exact headline and CTA copy. They usually bind these to fonts, color variables, icon choices, surface treatment such as glassmorphism, gradients, borders, and motion language. For Brandmint-style generation, produce brand strategy and copy first, then derive the visual system from it before section specs.

title: Asset contract encoded by prompts
text: Prompt output quality depends on supplying the right assets: hero video or poster, background images, logos, icons, fonts, product shots, GIF previews, testimonials, stats, and screenshots. Many prompts explicitly say to download remote assets at build time and serve locally. The asset plan should be treated as first-class input, not as an afterthought.

title: Copy specification pattern
text: Prompts either provide exact copy strings or define copy slots with tone and examples. Common slots are badge, headline, subtext, CTA labels, nav links, stats, testimonials, FAQ answers, pricing labels, and footer links. For automated generation, store copy slots separately from layout slots so the same structure can be rehydrated for different brands.

title: Motion and interaction specification pattern
text: Animation is usually specified in implementation terms: exact delays, easing curves, opacity and translate values, hover transforms, accordion timings, and scroll reveal behavior. Reusable primitives like FadeUp, BlurText, Typewriter, SpotlightBorder, and mobile menu overlays recur. The retrieval layer should detect when a brand needs subtle motion, cinematic motion, data motion, or playful motion and select prompt references accordingly.

title: Whole-site prompt blueprint
text: A whole-site prompt should be composed as: brief, tech contract, brand system, asset inventory, shared components, section order, section specs, responsive rules, behaviors, acceptance checks. A typical landing page sequence is navbar, hero, proof bar, feature blocks, process/how-it-works, stats, testimonials, pricing or CTA, FAQ, footer. This is the right abstraction level for Brandmint website generation.

title: How to use these prompts in embeddings
text: Index prompts as layered references instead of raw blobs only: corpus-level grammar, archetype-level blueprints, section-level patterns, asset heuristics, and copy slots. Use metadata keys like scope, category, type, brand archetype, motion style, asset types, and dependencies. Retrieve first by scope and brand archetype, then by section type, then by visual treatment.

title: Brand-to-asset planning heuristic
text: Luxury, agency, and editorial brands usually need cinematic hero video, serif display font, minimal nav, refined typography, case-study imagery, social proof, and tasteful glass or blur surfaces. SaaS and AI brands usually need UI screenshots, dashboard imagery, benchmark stats, icon systems, explainer sections, product motion, and pricing/FAQ. Real-estate and lifestyle brands need immersive photography or video, trust stats, property or product galleries, and concierge-style CTA copy. Contact and form sections need validation states, friendly reassurance copy, and brand-colored success/error signals.
